mcqs.question: What does a 'precise exception' guarantee?
options: That the exception handler runs in exactly one clock cycle
That the pipeline is flushed and restarted from the beginning of the program
That exceptions can only be raised by memory instructions
That every instruction before the faulting one has completed, the faulting one made no visible changes, and every instruction after it looks as if it never started
mcqs.explanation: Precise exceptions are about making the visible machine state look exactly as if execution stopped cleanly at one well-defined instruction boundary — older instructions fully done, the faulting instruction and everything younger not yet visible. It says nothing about handler speed, doesn't restrict which instructions can fault, and doesn't restart the whole program.

mcqs.question: What mechanism does flushing younger instructions after a confirmed exception resemble?
options: A branch-misprediction flush
A cache eviction
A structural-hazard stall
A TLB miss
mcqs.explanation: Both cases discard speculative-looking in-flight work that must never be allowed to commit — a branch misprediction flushes wrongly-fetched instructions, and an exception flushes younger instructions once an older fault is confirmed. Cache eviction, structural stalls, and TLB misses are unrelated mechanisms.

mcqs.question: How does in-order commit enable precise exceptions even when different exceptions are detected in different pipeline stages?
options: By preventing any instruction from ever raising an exception
By holding every instruction's write-back until all older instructions have already committed, so a younger instruction can never become visible ahead of an older fault
By running all instructions through the same pipeline stage simultaneously
By requiring the compiler to reorder instructions so faults never occur out of order
mcqs.explanation: In-order commit delays making any instruction's result permanently visible until every instruction before it has already committed cleanly — so even if a younger instruction technically finishes its computation first, it never becomes visible ahead of an older one that later turns out to have faulted. It doesn't prevent exceptions, doesn't merge stages, and isn't a compiler responsibility.

mcqs.question: Instructions A (older) and B (younger) are both in flight, and B's exception is detected first because it reached its fault-checking stage sooner. Which exception should the hardware report?
options: B's, since it was detected first
Both, simultaneously
A's, since it is the older instruction and the program never actually validly reached B's point of execution
Neither — the pipeline should simply resume execution
mcqs.explanation: Precise exceptions must respect program order, not detection order. Since A is older, the program logically never reaches B's fault in a correct execution — A's exception must be handled first (which then flushes B for possible re-execution afterward). Reporting B's exception, or both, or ignoring the situation would all break the precise-exception guarantee.

mcqs.question: Why does a page fault re-execute the faulting instruction after the handler runs, while an illegal opcode does not?
options: A page fault's cause (the missing page) can be fixed by the OS, so retrying the instruction now succeeds; an illegal opcode has no fix to apply and the process is terminated instead
Page faults are always detected earlier in the pipeline than illegal opcodes, so they're cheaper to retry
Illegal opcodes are precise exceptions while page faults are imprecise, so only page faults can safely restart
The hardware picks retry versus terminate at random depending on which stage detected the fault
mcqs.explanation: The retry-vs-terminate choice depends on whether the OS can remove the cause: mapping in the missing page fixes a page fault, so re-running the load now works. An illegal opcode has no such fix, so the OS terminates the process instead. Both are precise exceptions -- precision is about clean machine state, not about which action the handler takes afterward.
